name: London Plane
research_notes: All fields left empty after round 2. Woodland Trust's London plane page has no edible, medicinal or toxic content (only says fruit hairs aid wind dispersal); NC State's page likewise. Plane hairs and pollen are an allergy/airway irritant (search turned up a PubMed review on plane-tree sensitisation, 33603882, and a CDC-hosted Sydney study), but that is allergy, not poisoning, so not added to the poisonous layer. Suggest keeping off all three layers and merging with the 'Plane' row into one ^platanus row.

name: Monterey Cypress
poisonous: Mainly a risk to livestock. Cattle that eat the foliage, often from fallen or cut branches, can lose their calves in late pregnancy, and some cows become very ill or die. The likely cause is a resin acid in the leaves. No poisoning of people is recorded in these sources.
research_notes: Abortion in cattle: Massey University NZ poisonous plants database, Gardner/Parton PubMed abstract (16031906) and the 1996 NZ Vet J paper (sciquest), plus USDA ARS which says Monterey cypress 'may also cause abortions when eaten by cattle'. Illness/death of cows: Massey only (says abortion and death 'not uncommon'); the PubMed abstract only says abortion. Drop 'some cows become very ill or die' if you want strict two-source wording. 'Fallen branches' from Massey only; it is framed as context. The 'no poisoning of people recorded in these sources' sentence is an absence statement. This row must be tested BEFORE the Cupressus row. Bare 'macrocarpa' word is safe in this dataset (no other species with that epithet), but remove it if other macrocarpa species (e.g. Quercus macrocarpa, bur oak) are ever added.

name: Deodar
medicinal: In India and nearby countries the wood, bark and oil of deodar have long been used in traditional medicine, including Ayurveda, for dozens of different illnesses. Lab studies on extracts show some activity, but there are no good human trials, so its benefits and safety are unproven.
research_notes: Medicinal sources: Bisht et al. 2021 review in Journal of Ethnopharmacology (opened via its FAO AGRIS record, as NCBI was blocking access) and a 2025 review in J Ayurveda Integr Med Sci; PFAF as supporting third. Specific ailments (joints, coughs, skin) dropped: only one source each. Edible and poisonous left empty: PFAF lists no edible uses and no known hazards, and I found nothing else. Atlas Cedar (Cedrus atlantica, input9), Cedar-of-Lebanon, Cyprus cedar and plain 'Cedar' (Cedrus) are separate or unmatched; consider a single 'Cedar' row matching ^cedrus\b|\bcedar\b (but beware 'Incense-cedar' = Calocedrus and Thuja 'red cedar', which a \bcedar\b match would catch).

name: Cedar-of-Lebanon
research_notes: All fields left empty. Leads checked: a peer-reviewed ethnobotany paper (J Ethnobiol Ethnomed 2014, 10:29, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1746-4269-10-29) reviews folk use of Cedrus libani wood tar on skin, wounds and for colds in Turkey; the only second source found (Efe 2022, Furniture and Wooden Material Research Journal) has been RETRACTED, so not used. PFAF claims remain single-source. Suggest merging with the other Cedrus rows.

name: Oriental Plane
research_notes: All fields left empty. One search for traditional-medicine sources on Platanus orientalis found only PFAF, a USDA phytochemical database entry, Ayurveda/wiki sites and an unverified Bentham abstract - nothing that gives a second reputable source for PFAF's remedies. Not well documented enough for the medicinal layer. Hair irritation: see London Plane comment. Regex order: the generic Plane row will catch this species first unless this row is tested before it.

name: Plane
research_notes: Covers Platanus, Oriental Plane (P. orientalis) and American Plane (P. occidentalis). Nothing well sourced for any layer (see London Plane). The ^ anchor stops 'Acer pseudoplatanus' (Sycamore) and 'Acer platanoides' (Norway maple) matching; do NOT drop the anchor. \bplane\b will not match 'Sycamore'. Regex problem noticed elsewhere in species-mapping.txt: Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus) and Carpinus currently fall under the Pine row, presumably because a 'pinus' pattern matches inside 'Carpinus'; the Pine regex should be anchored, e.g. ^pinus\b.

name: Lawson's Cypress
research_notes: Left empty. Massey University's NZ poisonous plants site lists Chamaecyparis lawsoniana among trees containing isocupressic acid (cattle abortion) (https://poisonousplants.massey.ac.nz/plantToxins/isocupr.html), but I could not find a second reputable source, so dropped. The Botanical Dermatology Database (https://botanical-dermatology-database.info/BotDermFolder/CUPR.html) says some authors report skin rashes from the foliage but that the evidence is not convincing, so dropped too. Could be merged with the Chamaecyparis row.

name: Leyland Cypress
poisonous: Not known to be seriously poisonous. A few cases of skin rash (contact dermatitis) have been recorded in people handling the bark or planting the tree. Gloves and long sleeves are sensible when cutting Leyland hedges.
research_notes: Evidence is thin (DermNet: 'contact dermatitis to the bark has been recorded'; BoDD: one case report from planting). The last sentence is common-sense advice following from the rash claim, not a separate sourced claim; drop it if you want strictly sourced text only. Massey's NZ poisonous plants site lists Leyland cypress as containing isocupressic acid (cattle abortion), but only one source, so dropped. DermNet also says its pollen is a growing cause of asthma/hay fever in the Mediterranean (one source only, dropped). Leyland cypress and 'X Cupressocyparis' are the same plant (x Cupressocyparis leylandii, now Cuprocyparis / Hesperotropsis x leylandii); suggest merging the two rows with match: leylandii|\bleyland\b|cupressocyparis|cuprocyparis.

name: X Cupressocyparis
poisonous: Not known to be seriously poisonous. A few cases of skin rash (contact dermatitis) have been recorded in people handling the bark or planting this tree (Leyland cypress). Gloves and long sleeves are sensible when cutting these hedges.
research_notes: x Cupressocyparis in London street-tree data is almost always Leyland cypress (x Cupressocyparis leylandii); notes copied from that row. Suggest merging with Leyland Cypress. Note 'cupressocyparis' does not contain 'cupressus', so it will not be caught by the Cupressus regex below.

name: Tree-of-heaven
medicinal: The dried bark has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine, and in Korea and India, for problems including asthma and epilepsy. Laboratory studies are exploring its extracts, but there is little evidence from studies in people and more research is needed on whether it works and is safe.
poisonous: Not usually eaten, but the sap can irritate skin and cause a rash in some people. Very rarely, sap getting into cuts has been linked to inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis) in people felling the trees. The pollen can trigger allergies. Wear gloves if handling cut stems.
research_notes: FEIS (Other Uses section, around characters 100k-200k of the page) covers sap dermatitis, the hospitalised tree-remover case, pollen allergy, and the medicinal uses (stem bark for diarrhoea/dysentery, root bark for epilepsy and asthma). The Li et al. 2021 J Ethnopharmacol review gives asthma and epilepsy among the traditional uses of the bark ('Chunpi') and says more efficacy and safety studies are needed. Dropped (one source only): diarrhoea/dysentery use (FEIS only), toxicity of bark at high doses (review only). Harvard Health has an article on the myocarditis link but it is paywalled, so not cited. 'Little evidence from studies in people' is my summary of the review's statement that only a few traditional uses match the pharmacology findings and that more studies are needed. Invasive species; edible use not supported. Regex: 'tree.of.heaven' matches 'Tree-of-heaven' and 'tree of heaven'.

name: Tulip-tree
medicinal: In North America the bark was once used in folk medicine, for example as a tonic for rheumatism and indigestion. These are historical uses only. It is not a modern herbal medicine, and there is no good evidence that it works.
research_notes: FEIS: tonic for rheumatism and dyspepsia from stem bark, heart stimulant from root inner bark (late 1800s). USDA Ethnobotanical database: rheumatism, dyspepsia, fever, malaria etc. NC State: Native Americans used inner bark for cough and cholera. Only rheumatism/indigestion have two sources, so other uses dropped. 'No good evidence that it works' is an absence claim: no source tests it and none of the sources reports modern evidence; delete that clause if you want strictly sourced wording. Consider whether this row belongs on the medicinal layer at all; it is weak. NC State tags it non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses, so poisonous left empty. Could not open PMC (CAPTCHA) or a valid PFAF page (pfaf.org returned the wrong plant), so neither cited. Regex avoids matching unrelated 'tulip' names; there is no other tulip-tree species in the mapping.

name: Cupressus
research_notes: Covers Cupressus (unspecified), Italian Cypress (C. sempervirens), Arizona Cypress (C. arizonica) and Smooth Arizona-Cypress (Hesperocyparis glabra). Monterey Cypress (C. macrocarpa) has its own row; make sure that row is tested BEFORE this one, or this regex will grab it. Nothing true for all species with two sources: Massey lists C. sempervirens with isocupressic acid (cattle abortion) and BoDD says Italian cypress wood can cause dermatitis, each single-source only. Did not use a bare \bcypress\b because it would catch Swamp Cypress (Taxodium), Cypress Oak (Quercus robur fastigiata), Lawson/Leyland/Nootka/Sawara/Hinoki cypresses.

name: Atlas Cedar
research_notes: No well-sourced content. NC State's Cedrus atlantica page has no toxicity/edible/medicinal information (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cedrus-atlantica/). Cedarwood essential oil is used in aromatherapy, but I found no reputable medical source. Suggest one Cedar row for all true cedars with ^cedrus\b (Atlas, Deodar, Cedar-of-Lebanon, Cyprus Cedar, Cedar); avoid a bare 'cedar' pattern, which would catch Western Red-cedar (Thuja), Japanese Red-cedar (Cryptomeria) and Incense-cedar (Calocedrus), which are not true cedars.

name: Chamaecyparis
research_notes: Covers Chamaecyparis, Lawson's, Sawara (C. pisifera) and Hinoki (C. obtusa) cypresses. Nothing with two reputable sources (see Lawson's Cypress). Nootka Cypress is now Xanthocyparis nootkatensis and will not match. Could merge Lawson's Cypress into this row.

name: Indian-bean-tree
medicinal: In North American folk medicine the bark was used as a laxative and to expel worms, and as a stand-in for quinine against malaria. Leaves and seeds were also used for skin problems and coughs. These are historical uses with no good modern evidence, and the roots are poisonous.
poisonous: The roots are described as highly poisonous. Little detail is published on symptoms or cases. The long bean-like pods are not a food. Keep children and pets from chewing roots or pods.
research_notes: Root toxicity: USDA NRCS Plant Guide and PFAF both say 'roots are highly poisonous', but both trace to the same book (Chevallier 1996) and give no symptoms or cases, so I set risk to moderate rather than high; your call. 'Pods are not a food': PFAF says edible uses 'none known' and the USDA guide lists none; there is no source saying the pods are poisonous, so the warning about chewing pods is caution, not a sourced toxicity claim. Edit it out if you prefer. Medicinal: laxative and vermifuge in all three sources; quinine substitute in USDA guide and PFAF; skin uses in USDA guide and USDA ethnobotany database; cough uses (seed tea for asthma/bronchitis, whooping cough) only in USDA guide, so 'coughs' is weakly supported (one source); remove 'and coughs' to be strict. 'No good modern evidence' is my summary; the USDA guide mentions only unspecified 'modern pharmaceutical research' on diuretic effects. Covers the 'Catalpa' row too (^catalpa\b).

name: Dawn Redwood
research_notes: No edible, medicinal or toxic content found. NC State's page has nothing on toxicity, edibility or medicinal use (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/metasequoia-glyptostroboides/). Keep off all layers. Regex anchored so it won't catch Sequoia or Sequoiadendron.

name: Pride-of-India
research_notes: All fields left empty. Edible: University of Arizona Campus Arboretum and PFAF say the seeds are edible roasted (and PFAF says leaves cooked), but Arizona adds they are 'not commonly consumed', so it fails the 'genuinely eaten in practice' test. Medicinal: only PFAF (flowers used for eye complaints/conjunctivitis in Chinese medicine), so dropped. Poisonous: Arizona lists toxicity as 'benign', PFAF 'none known'; NC State gives no toxicity entry. Sources opened: https://apps.cals.arizona.edu/arboretum/taxon.aspx?id=370 , https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Koelreuteria%20paniculata , https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/koelreuteria-paniculata . Regex: deliberately avoids plain 'golden rain' because that is also a Laburnum name.

name: Pinaceae
research_notes: All fields left empty on purpose. 'Pinaceae' is a whole family (pines, spruces, firs, cedars, larches, hemlocks, Douglas fir), so the tree could be any of them, and no edible or medicinal claim is true for all. Do not reuse the pine-needle tea or spruce-tip notes here: the reader cannot tell which tree it is. Suggest either showing a generic line ('a conifer in the pine family; species not recorded') or leaving it off the layers. No research was done beyond checking the mapping.

name: Persian Ironwood
research_notes: All fields left empty: no edible, medicinal or toxicity information found. The PFAF page for Parrotia persica did not load properly.

name: Caucasian Wingnut
research_notes: All fields left empty. PFAF says the seed is edible but 'very small and would be very fiddly to use' (not food in practice) and lists one single-source medicinal word ('diaphoretic'); known hazards 'none known'. The regex also catches the 2-tree 'Pterocarya' entry, which currently falls under no row.

name: Hornbeam
medicinal: In folk medicine hornbeam leaves were used on cuts to stop bleeding and help wounds heal. There are no scientific studies showing that this works.
research_notes: REGEX BUG: Hornbeam (1,629 trees) and 'Carpinus' currently fall under the Pine row because its regex 'pinus' matches inside 'Carpinus'. Fix the Pine regex to \bpine\b|^pinus\b (and test this Hornbeam row before Pine). The new Hornbeam regex is anchored so it does NOT catch 'Hop Hornbeam' (Ostrya carpinifolia) or 'Zelkova carpinifolia'. Medicinal: the second sentence is a statement of what I could not find, not a sourced claim; drop it if you prefer. Woodland Trust also mentions a hornbeam tonic for tiredness (single source, dropped). Edible and poisonous: PFAF says none known for both; Woodland Trust mentions only wildlife eating the seeds.

name: Hop Hornbeam
research_notes: All fields left empty: PFAF lists no edible uses, no medicinal uses and no known hazards, and I found nothing else. Regex also catches the 1-tree 'Ostrya' entry.

name: Plum yew
medicinal: Plum yews contain alkaloids that kill cancer cells. A drug based on one of them, omacetaxine (homoharringtonine), is approved in the US for a type of leukaemia when other drugs fail. This is a hospital drug made in a lab, not a herbal remedy.
research_notes: REGEX BUG: the single Cephalotaxus tree currently falls under the Yew row because 'taxus' matches inside 'Cephalotaxus'. Fix the Yew regex to \byew\b|^taxus\b and test this row before Yew (note 'Plum yew' also contains \byew\b). Poisonous left EMPTY because sources disagree: NC State Plant Toolbox says seeds and foliage are 'quite poisonous' (but names taxine, the yew toxin, which looks copied from Taxus), while PFAF lists no known hazards and says the seed is eaten. Edible left empty: only PFAF says fruit/seed are eaten (and says the fruit of the type species is astringent); Harvard's Arnold Arboretum only mentions seed oil in Japan. Given the yew resemblance, keeping it off the edible layer seems wise. Cancer.gov confirms the US approval; the Springer review (Oncology and Therapy 2018) confirms the Cephalotaxus origin and FDA approval; Harvard confirms anticancer alkaloids in the plant. NCBI/PMC pages were blocked during this session. ROUND 2: re-searched toxicity; only NC State Plant Toolbox pages found (again naming taxine), so poisonous stays empty. Owner may prefer to show it on the poisonous layer as a precaution given NC State's warning, or leave the tree unmapped.

name: Dwarf / sour cherry
edible: Sour (Morello-type) cherries ripen in summer. Most people find them too sour raw, so they are usually cooked in pies, jams and sauces, or dried. Never eat the leaves, and don't crack or chew the stones.
medicinal: Tart cherry juice and extracts are sold as supplements, mainly for sleep and recovery after hard exercise. Some small trials and reviews show modest benefits, but results vary and researchers say more and better studies are needed.
poisonous: The kernel inside the stone contains a compound that turns into cyanide in the body. A whole stone swallowed by accident usually passes straight through, but chewed or crushed stones can cause poisoning.
research_notes: 'Too sour raw' is from Penn State Extension; PFAF calls the fruit 'pleasantly acid' and eatable raw, so the note says 'most people'. PFAF also says the seed can be eaten if not too bitter, which conflicts with poison advice: I have not repeated it. Poisonous field rests on poison.org (US National Capital Poison Center, about stone-fruit pits generally) plus PFAF (genus-wide cyanide warning); I could not open a peer-reviewed cherry-kernel paper (PMC blocked), so you may want a third source. 'Never eat the leaves' is supported by PFAF's genus warning only indirectly (PFAF actually lists leaves as a tea substitute): consider dropping that clause. Traditional bark remedies in PFAF are single-source, dropped. Regex order: the Ornamental cherry row ('cherry|prunus') will catch this tree unless this row is tested first.

name: Rum cherry
edible: Also called black cherry. The ripe dark cherries (late summer) can be eaten raw, though often bitter, or made into jelly and wine. Remove the stones. Leaves, twigs, bark and stones are not edible.
medicinal: The inner bark was a traditional North American cough remedy, and wild cherry syrups are still sold for coughs. There are no published human trials showing that it works.
poisonous: Leaves, twigs, bark and stones contain compounds that release cyanide. Wilted leaves, after storms or hedge cutting, are the most dangerous and can kill cattle, horses, sheep and goats quickly. For people, the main risk is from chewing or crushing the stones.
research_notes: Risk set to 'low' under the brief's definition (main danger is to livestock and horses), but it is a serious livestock risk; consider 'moderate' if you weight animals more. The 'no human trials' claim comes from the same Healthwise text published by University of Michigan Health and PeaceHealth, so it is effectively one source. The human-stone risk is supported by poison.org (stone fruits generally) and the USDA plant guide ('theoretical risk' from very large amounts). Regex order: the Ornamental cherry row ('cherry|prunus') will catch this tree unless this row is tested first. 'black cherry' in the regex is safe against the current mapping.

name: Yew
medicinal: Yew gave us important cancer drugs. Paclitaxel (Taxol) was first isolated from Pacific yew bark, and related compounds are now taken from European yew foliage to make these medicines in a lab. This is hospital chemotherapy, not a herbal remedy. Never use any part of a yew yourself.
poisonous: Leaves, bark and seeds are highly poisonous, including the seed inside the red 'berry'. Only the red flesh is not toxic. The poison upsets the heart's rhythm and can kill. Children have been seriously harmed. Extremely dangerous to horses, cattle, sheep and goats.
research_notes: Dropped '50-100g of needles can kill an adult' (only found on a magazine site, not two reputable sources) and 'clippings kill horses' (only Ontario ministry). Docetaxel detail dropped: sources say compounds for semi-synthesis come from European yew, but none I opened named docetaxel's source. REGEX/ROW PROBLEM: 'taxus' also matches 'Cephalotaxus' (plum yew, 1 tree), which is a different genus whose toxicity I could not source; suggest a stricter regex (e.g. \byew\b|\btaxus\b) and a separate row 'Plum yew' (Cephalotaxus) or leave it unmapped. Old sources (Cambridge Botanic Garden, Oxford herbaria, PFAF yew) could not be opened this session (permission not granted), so were not reused. ROUND 2: added British Horse Society poisonous-plants page (lists yew as deadly to horses) as an extra source for the horse claim. Edible left empty on purpose: the red flesh is not toxic, but the seed inside is, so it should not appear on the edible layer. Docetaxel and '50-100g' claims still not sourced twice.

name: Laburnum
poisonous: Every part is poisonous, especially the pea-like pods and seeds. Eating them causes vomiting and stomach upset; large amounts can bring on fits (convulsions), coma and breathing failure, and can kill. Children are at risk, so keep them away from the pods. Horses and livestock are also poisoned.
research_notes: ROUND 2: severe symptoms sourced from NC State (drowsiness, muscle spasms, coma, 'may be fatal'), BfR (convulsions, breathing paralysis) and Massey University (convulsions, coma, death). Children: Kent Wildlife Trust (seeds attract children) and Massey (children listed among those poisoned). Horses/livestock: NC State (goats, horses), Massey (all livestock incl. horses), British Horse Society. Dropped: dogs poisoned by chewing laburnum sticks (Massey only; ASPCA page blocked), 'small numbers of seeds often cause no symptoms' (NC State only). The 'Golden Chain Tree' entry's Latin 'Laburnum anagyroides alpinum' is probably Laburnum x watereri or L. alpinum; note fits all laburnums. Suggested latin: 'Laburnum spp.'.

name: Viburnum
poisonous: The blue-black berries are not food. Eaten, the plant can irritate the mouth and gut, causing drooling, vomiting and diarrhoea. Upsets are usually mild. Small children and pets are the most likely to eat the berries.
research_notes: RHS: 'fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten'. University of Zurich veterinary toxicology database lists V. tinus as toxic (salivation, vomiting, diarrhoea; toxic dose unknown). Victoria (Australia) agriculture page cites Mabberley ('poisonous fruit') and Brickell ('mild stomach upset'). The 'children and pets' line is a plain-sense reading of who eats berries, not a separately sourced claim; cut it if you want strict sourcing. NC State's V. tinus page says nothing on toxicity. Only Laurustinus falls under this row, so the notes fit. pfaf.org was blocked for this run, so the old source could not be re-checked.

name: Bay
edible: The leaves are the bay leaves of cooking. They are used fresh or dried to flavour soups and stews, as a flavouring rather than eaten whole. Poisonous plants have been mistaken for bay. Cherry laurel, a common hedge plant, has similar leaves that release cyanide.
poisonous: Oils in the leaves can cause vomiting and diarrhoea in dogs, cats and horses. Swallowing a lot of whole leaves can block the gut.
research_notes: Look-alike: the Toxins paper (MDPI) says cherry laurel leaves look like bay and are confused with it; the second source for misidentification (Toxicology Reports, via DOAJ) is an oleander-mistaken-for-bay case, so the note says 'poisonous plants' in general and names cherry laurel as the local example. Cherry laurel toxicity itself is backed by MDPI + NC State. A food reference on ckbk.com (unnamed work) also states cherry laurel is confused with bay, but it is not on the approved list so not cited. NC State says the leaves 'should not be eaten' (choking/cuts) - single source, so softened to 'flavouring rather than eaten whole'. pfaf.org could not be opened (permission request timed out), so the old PFAF source is not used. The old MDPI source is kept. NC State rates bay 'low' severity for people. Round 2: no changes; round-1 content kept as properly sourced. No medicinal search done (no EMA monograph for Laurus nobilis known; budget used elsewhere).

name: Cherry laurel / Portugal laurel
poisonous: Leaves, stems and seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides. These release cyanide when the plant is chewed or crushed. Wilting leaves, such as hedge clippings, are especially dangerous. Farm animals such as cattle can be killed, and dogs, cats and horses are also at risk. The leaves can be mistaken for bay leaves used in cooking.
research_notes: Covers both P. laurocerasus and P. lusitanica: the Zurich vet toxicology database rates both 'strongly toxic'; NC State rates laurocerasus 'high' but lusitanica 'low' severity (disagreement noted; kept risk high). Dropped 'smells of almonds' (only found as a general cyanide sign in animals' breath). Bay confusion supported by the Toxins 2022 paper (poisonings from mistaking cherry laurel for bay) and North Wales Wildlife Trust ('not to be confused with bay'). Toxins paper says severe human poisoning is rare and mainly affects children (single source, not used). ASPCA page is for Prunus spp. generally. Fruit flesh is low in cyanogens per Zurich and NC State says ripe P. lusitanica fruit is edible, but I did not add any edible claim. Could not open the RHS harmful-plants page or the Massey laurel page (permission request timed out). ROUND 2: no changes; row already well sourced. | FACT-CHECK: poisonous reworded after independent check ('Cattle have died after eating them [hedge clippings]' is only in one source (Irish Vet J case report PMC7989689, 36 weanlings near a laurel hedge and clippings)

name: Horse chestnut
medicinal: A standardised extract of common horse chestnut seeds, with the toxin removed, is used for chronic venous insufficiency (aching, swollen legs from weak leg veins). EU regulators accept this use in adults, and trial reviews suggest it eases symptoms short term, though bigger trials are needed. Raw seeds, leaves, bark and flowers are unsafe to take.
poisonous: All parts are poisonous, especially the conkers (seeds). Eating them causes stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea; children may also become weak or drowsy. Dogs, cats and horses are at risk too. Don't confuse with sweet chestnut: its case has many fine spines and holds two or three pointed nuts, while a conker is single, round and glossy.
research_notes: Medicinal note deliberately says 'common horse chestnut': the extract evidence is for A. hippocastanum only, not the red, Indian or buckeye species also on this row. Toxicity is genus-wide (ASPCA page is filed under Aesculus glabra; NC State rates A. hippocastanum high severity, 'may be fatal'); I kept risk moderate because poison.org says severe adult cases are rare. Dropped (single-source): pregnancy warning (NCCIH only), bleeding/blood-thinner interaction (MSKCC only), 'aescin' name in the public note. The input's nccih.nih.gov/health/horse-chestnut URL could not be fetched directly; the equivalent nccih.nih.gov/health/horsechestnut was opened instead. ROUND 2: added EMA herbal monograph page (well-established use for chronic venous insufficiency, adults only). Pregnancy warning still single-source (EMA page silent; MedlinePlus page failed; nccih.nih.gov/health/horse-chestnut blocked).

name: Sweet chestnut
edible: The shiny brown nuts fall in spiny cases in October. They can be eaten raw but are usually roasted, then peeled. Do not confuse them with conkers from horse chestnut, which are poisonous: sweet chestnut cases have many fine spines and hold two or three nuts; conkers are usually single.
research_notes: Dropped: 'score the shell so they don't burst' (only the Woodland Trust October foraging blog says it); 'London street trees give small nuts' (only Forestry England notes the UK climate is often too cold for nuts to ripen well); 'raw nuts high in tannin' (no source found). Raw is edible per Forestry England and Wild Food UK. Horse-chestnut look-alike warning added (Woodland Trust conker blog + Poison Control US). pfaf leaf medicinal uses not added (single source). Original pfaf URL could not be opened at first attempt. | FACT-CHECK: edible reworded after independent check ('Baked or boiled' appears only in the Woodland Trust October blog. Other claims supported: October fall (WT blog, NC State), raw (Forestry England, Wild Food UK)

name: Walnut
edible: Nuts ripen in autumn, when the green husk splits. They are eaten raw or roasted. Unripe green walnuts, picked before the shell inside hardens, are pickled. The husks stain skin dark brown, so wear gloves. Black walnut nuts are edible too, but very hard to crack.
medicinal: Common walnut leaf is a traditional European remedy, used on the skin for mild inflammation and for sweaty hands and feet. Leaves and husks were also used as astringents (drying, tightening agents) in folk medicine. These uses rest on long tradition, not good clinical trials.
poisonous: Mainly a risk to animals. Fresh black walnut shavings or sawdust used as bedding can cause laminitis (a painful hoof disease) in horses. Fallen walnuts that go mouldy can carry fungal toxins that cause vomiting, tremors and seizures in dogs.
research_notes: Old pfaf URL format (pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?...) was blocked; the new-format pfaf page was used instead. Row covers Juglans regia and J. nigra (Black Walnut, 35 trees). Edible and poisonous notes are written to cover both. The medicinal note is about common walnut (J. regia) only, as the EMA monograph covers that species; EMA also says adults only and not on open wounds, but I found no second source for those so dropped them. Dropped from the old text: June as the green-walnut picking month (RHS and pfaf give no month) and 'stain for days'. The horse laminitis evidence is for black walnut (both sources); neither covers common walnut. The Ontario page also says mouldy fallen walnuts can poison livestock. Juglone (from roots and leaves) harms other plants, not people, so left out.

name: Pecan / hickory
edible: Pecan and shagbark hickory nuts are sweet and edible, eaten as nuts or used in baking and sweets. Pecans need a long, hot growing season to ripen their nuts, so trees in a cooler climate like London's rarely crop well.
research_notes: Not every Carya has good nuts: NC State says bitternut hickory (Carya cordiformis) nuts are very bitter (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/carya-cordiformis/), but I found only one source, so left it out. The generic 'Carya' tree may not be pecan or shagbark. 'Raw or roasted' dropped (not stated by two sources). USDA plant guide lists Native American medicinal uses (leaves for ringworm, bark for TB) - single source, minor, omitted. Latin in species list is spelled 'illinoensis'; accepted spelling is illinoinensis (keep regex on \bcarya).

name: Witch hazel
medicinal: Extracts of the leaves and bark, including distilled witch hazel water, are a traditional remedy for mild inflammation of the skin, mouth and throat. They are still sold today. Regulators accept this because of long use, not because of strong trials, and good clinical evidence is limited. They can occasionally irritate the skin or cause an allergic rash.
research_notes: No witch hazel appears in species-mapping.txt, so this row currently matches no trees on the map. The 'bruises' claim was dropped: no second source. The EMA document I opened is the 2008 draft monograph. The final EU monograph has the same traditional-use basis, according to the 2025 Molecules review (the MDPI paper, also at PMC12250947). Health Canada covers mouth and throat use; EMA and the review cover skin use.

name: Hazel
edible: Common hazel, filbert and Turkish hazel all have edible nuts. Most ripen in September and October, when the husks turn yellow-brown. They can be roasted. Turkish hazel nuts are small and thick-shelled, inside a spiky husk. Squirrels often take them first. Hazelnuts are a common nut allergen.
research_notes: Claim-to-source map. Edible nuts: Woodland Trust and RHS (common hazel, filbert); NC State, Virginia Tech and Utah State (Turkish hazel). Sept-Oct and husk colour: Woodland Trust blog and RHS ('husks begin to turn yellow around late September'). Roasted: Woodland Trust blog and NC State. Small, thick shell, spiky husk: NC State, Virginia Tech, Utah State. Squirrels: RHS and Woodland Trust blog. Allergen: NHS, Allergy UK, UHL NHS leaflet (which also names filberts and cobnuts). Dropped 'eat raw' (only the Woodland Trust blog says it). Only folk charm 'uses' found for medicine, so medicinal is left empty. The regex 'hazel' would also catch 'witch hazel' (Hamamelis) if it ever appears in the data; it is not in the current species list. Consider 'hazel(?!.*witch)' or '(?<!witch[ -])hazel'.

name: Monkey puzzle
edible: Trees are either male or female, and only female trees carry the big spiny cones. These release large brown seeds, which are edible. In Chile the seeds are a traditional food, eaten boiled or roasted.
research_notes: Dropped 'Most London trees don't produce them' - no source found. Seeds-edible: Woodland Trust + Pirineos (CSIC peer-reviewed journal on Pewenche/settler use of pinon). 'Boiled or roasted': Pirineos + Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste (not on the approved list but a reputable food-heritage body; owner may want to replace it). Male/female: Woodland Trust (dioecious) + RBGE (one male, one female tree producing seed). Flour use dropped (only one source). pfaf.org not opened (permission blocked).

name: Stone pine
edible: The seeds are pine nuts (pinoli), a food in the Mediterranean for over 2,000 years. They grow inside the large cones, which take about three years to ripen. The nuts are rich in fat and protein and are used in cooking and sweets.
research_notes: Sources: EUFORGEN/IPGRI technical guidelines (cones mature in about 3 years), CIHEAM/FAO Options Mediterraneennes paper and a CyTA Journal of Food paper (Mediterranean diet, composition, cooking and confectionery), Annals of Forest Science (edible nuts; 3-year-old cones, 42-month reproductive cycle). The Gymnosperm Database (conifers.org) also confirms 3-year ripening but is not on the approved list, so not cited. PFAF page returned the wrong plant (yew) when fetched, so not cited. Regex: 'umbrella pine' also matches Japanese umbrella pine (Sciadopitys verticillata), which is unrelated and has no edible nuts; suggest removing 'umbrella pine' from match. Unrelated row issue spotted in species-mapping.txt: Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus) and 'Carpinus' are mapped to the Pine row, almost certainly because 'carPINUS' contains 'pinus'; the Pine regex needs a word boundary (\bpinus).

name: Pine
edible: Young pine needles can be steeped in hot water as a tea, and pine-needle drinks were used in the past against scurvy. Scots pine inner bark was dried and ground into flour in northern Europe. Be sure it is a pine: its needles grow in bundles of 2 to 5. Very poisonous yew has flat needles that grow singly.
medicinal: Pine needles and resin have long been folk remedies for coughs and colds, often breathed in as steam, and pine needle oil is inhaled for breathing problems. These are traditional uses; they have not been properly tested in clinical trials.
research_notes: REGEX BUG: 'pinus' matches inside 'Carpinus', so Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus, 1,629 trees) and Carpinus (2) are mapped to Pine. Fix with \bpinus\b (and keep \bpine\b). Removed the claim that needle tea is 'rich in vitamin C': a peer-reviewed study of Scots pine needles (redalyc link) found vitamin C 'rather low' compared with other sources, highest in winter. Pregnancy warning on pine needle tea (Durham Wildlife Trust) refers to ponderosa pine; USDA/extension sources link ponderosa and lodgepole needles to cattle abortions, but none of those species is on the London list, so no poisonous note. Clinical-evidence statement in medicinal rests mainly on the Frontiers review; PFAF just lists traditional uses. Inner-bark flour is sourced for Scots pine only.

name: Spruce / fir
edible: In spring the soft, light-green new tips of spruce and fir (including Douglas fir) are eaten raw or used to flavour syrups, teas and drinks such as spruce beer. Be certain it is not yew, whose flat needles look similar and are deadly poisonous.
medicinal: Shoots, needles and resin were used in folk medicine for coughs, colds and chest complaints, and young shoots against scurvy (vitamin C lack). Evidence comes mainly from tradition and lab tests, not clinical trials, and one study found the shoots hold less vitamin C than often claimed.
research_notes: Row covers Picea, Abies, Pseudotsuga and (via 'spruce') Western Hemlock-spruce Tsuga heterophylla. Edibility of Tsuga tips rests only on Wild Food UK, so hemlock is not named in the note; consider excluding Tsuga from the regex or a separate row, and beware readers confusing 'hemlock' tree with poisonous hemlock (Conium, not sourced here). Yew look-alike: only Wild Food UK explicitly says yew needles resemble fir/Douglas fir; Woodland Trust and NC State confirm yew's flat needles and deadly toxicity. Scurvy claim: Raal et al. 2018 (redalyc) for spruce shoots; pfaf for vitamin C-rich tea; Raal et al. also call the 'rich in vitamin C' idea partly a myth. PMC7570650 notes piperidine alkaloids in spruce sprouts may pose a health risk at some exposures (single source, not added). Suggest latin 'Picea / Abies / Pseudotsuga'. UW Miller Library page advises against gathering needles from urban trees (pollution) - single source.

name: Juniper
edible: Common juniper's 'berries' (really soft cones) take about 18 months or more to ripen from green to blue-black. Ripe berries are a spice, used to flavour gin, meat dishes and cabbage. Common juniper is the species normally used, so don't assume other junipers in the map are the same.
medicinal: Juniper berry is a traditional herbal remedy to increase urine flow and ease indigestion and wind. This rests on long use, not good clinical trials. Official guidance says not to use it in pregnancy or with kidney disease.
research_notes: Row covers Juniperus (unspecified, 18), J. communis (12), J. virginiana (11), J. chinensis (1). Edible and medicinal notes are worded for common juniper only. Sources disagree on the others: NC State lists J. virginiana berries as low-toxicity and gives no food use, but says J. chinensis cones are edible (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/juniperus-chinensis/). Consider splitting: 'Common juniper' (Juniperus communis) on edible/medicinal layers, and 'Other junipers' (Juniperus virginiana, Juniperus chinensis, Juniperus spp.) with no edible note. Dropped the old savin (J. sabina) warning: I could not open two reputable sources in this run, and savin is not in the map. Poisonous left empty: NC State rates J. communis and J. virginiana as low toxicity (large amounts may cause diarrhoea) and its communis page also says large doses can harm the kidneys. But both pages are from one database and I found no second source. The pregnancy warning is in the medicinal field (EMA: not recommended; Health Canada: do not use). EMA also says not for under-18s (single source, dropped).

name: Thuja (red cedar)
poisonous: Leaves, twigs and cones contain thujone, an oil that is toxic if swallowed. Eating the plant can cause stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Large amounts, especially brewed as a tea, can cause fits. Keep children and pets from chewing it.
research_notes: BfR (German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment) is the only source I opened that describes Thuja symptoms directly; UC ANR confirms Thuja is toxic if eaten because of thujone and warns about children and pets; EMA and MedlinePlus (cedar leaf oil) support thujone causing vomiting and fits. Dropped: sap irritating skin/eyes and liver/kidney damage (BfR only). Medicinal left empty: NC State notes twig teas for constipation/headache and Thuja is used in homeopathy, but not two reputable sources with evidence. Regex: 'western red cedar' will not match 'Western Red-cedar' (hyphen); it is caught by 'thuja' in the Latin anyway. Suggest 'western red.?cedar'. 'Japanese Red-cedar' (Cryptomeria) correctly not matched.

name: Holly
poisonous: The red berries are the main danger. They cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Most cases are young children, and a few berries can be enough to cause symptoms. Most cases are mild. The berries are also poisonous to pets.
research_notes: REGEX PROBLEM: the match 'holly|ilex' also catches Evergreen Oak, Quercus ilex (356 trees), which is wrongly mapped to Holly. Suggest anchoring the match, e.g. 'holly|ilex aquifolium|^ilex', or adding a 'Holm oak' row (Quercus ilex, match 'evergreen oak|holm oak|quercus ilex') placed before Holly, or folding it into the Oak row. INCHEM (WHO) gives an old 'lethal dose' of 20 to 30 berries but says no recent case confirms it, so I left out any mention of death.

name: Box
poisonous: All parts, especially the leaves, contain alkaloids. In people, eating it may cause stomach cramps, sickness and diarrhoea, but serious poisoning is rare. The sap can mildly irritate skin. It is more dangerous to animals: dogs, cats and horses. Livestock eating leaves or dumped hedge clippings have had fits and died.
research_notes: Risk changed from moderate to low. The brief's scale puts 'mild for people, or a risk mainly to animals' at low. NC State rates it 'low severity', and US Poison Control says it is generally of low toxicity for humans. If you weight the livestock deaths more heavily, moderate is defensible. Claim-to-source map. Alkaloids: NC State, ASPCA, Massey ('all parts'). Human stomach upset: NC State and Poison Control. Skin irritation: NC State and Poison Control. Dogs, cats, horses: ASPCA and Poison Control. Livestock fits and death: Massey (which also mentions hedge trimmings dumped in paddocks) and Poison Control. The 'especially the leaves' part rests on NC State (leaves named as the toxic part) and Massey (highest levels in stem and leaves). Tried the PMC review 'Alkaloid-containing plants poisonous to cattle and horses in Europe' (PMC4690134), but it was behind a browser check and its abstract does not mention Buxus, so it is not cited. Regex note: '\bbox\b' would also match 'Christmas box' (Sarcococca) if it ever appears in the data; it is not in the current list.

name: Privet
poisonous: The berries and leaves are poisonous if eaten. They can cause stomach pain, sickness and diarrhoea. Privet is also poisonous to dogs, cats and horses.
research_notes: Row covers Ligustrum vulgare, L. lucidum, L. ovalifolium and unspecified Ligustrum. NC State covers vulgare and lucidum (both 'medium' severity, fruits and leaves); UC ANR covers Ligustrum spp. generally ('berries and leaves are poisonous'); ASPCA lists L. vulgare and L. japonicum as toxic to dogs, cats and horses. No source specific to L. ovalifolium was opened, but the genus-level UC ANR page covers it. Dropped 'especially in children' (no source says children are more at risk; UC ANR only advises supervising children and pets). Dropped headache/weakness (only NC State). Ligustrum lucidum fruit is used in Chinese medicine but this was not researched and would not apply to the whole row. pfaf.org not opened.

name: Spindle
poisonous: All parts are poisonous, including the leaves and the colourful pink and orange fruits. Eating them can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, weakness and chills, and large amounts can lead to fits or coma. Poisoning is rare. Horses and other animals can also be poisoned.
research_notes: ROUND 2: Woodland Trust spindle page now opened: confirms leaves and fruit are toxic to people and laxative. It also says baked powdered fruit was used against head lice and mange in cattle - single reputable source, so no medicinal note. Changed risk from high to moderate: NC State rates severity 'low' and Massey University says poisonings are rare, though both list convulsions and coma after large amounts; owner may prefer high. Dropped 'heart problems': only Massey names cardiac glycosides (ASPCA mentions heart rhythm problems but for a different species, E. atropurpurea). 'Poisoning is rare' is Massey only (NC State 'low severity' is consistent). Animal claim: Massey (horses died, goats affected) plus ASPCA, whose 'spindle tree' entry is the American species E. atropurpurea, toxic to dogs, cats and horses. Could not open the RHS harmful-plants page. Regex 'euonymus' also catches evergreen garden Euonymus (e.g. E. japonicus), also listed as toxic by NC State, so the note still holds broadly.

name: Rhododendron
poisonous: All parts contain grayanotoxins, and honey made from the nectar ('mad honey') can carry them too. Eating leaves, flowers or this honey can cause vomiting, dizziness, a slow heartbeat and low blood pressure. Deaths in people are rare. Dogs, cats and horses are more likely to be seriously harmed.
research_notes: NC State rates R. ponticum toxicity 'low' while the PubMed reviews describe sometimes life-threatening heart effects in people; 'moderate' is a compromise. The review (PMID 22528814) says cattle and pets are killed more often than people; I named only dogs, cats and horses (also in ASPCA) because livestock had one source.

name: Photinia
poisonous: The leaves contain cyanogenic glycosides, which can release cyanide when chewed. The risk is mainly to grazing animals such as cattle and horses, and to pets, rather than people.
research_notes: Seed toxicity dropped (unsourced). Sources disagree: NC State (leaves cyanogenic, problem for horses and pets) and Burrows & Tyrl 1983, Bovine Practitioner (Photinia spp. among most important cyanogenic ornamentals for cattle) vs Extension.org horse Q&A ('not familiar with any harmful effects' of red-tip photinia) and pfaf ('none known'). Mapping uses the genus 'Photinia'; most London trees are likely Photinia x fraseri, so suggest latin 'Photinia'. pfaf leaf medicinal uses not added (single source).

name: Cotoneaster
poisonous: Berries, leaves and flowers contain small amounts of chemicals that release cyanide when digested. A few berries are unlikely to do harm, but large amounts can poison children and animals such as dogs and livestock, causing breathing trouble, weakness and, in severe cases, seizures.
research_notes: Sources differ on severity. CHOP Poison Control (US) says poisonous only in large amounts. Massey University (NZ) says toxicity needs large intakes and the outlook is good after small amounts. UC ANR's drought-planting list calls it 'highly poisonous if ingested', with no detail. I kept risk at low because two sources say harm needs large amounts. You could raise it to moderate to be cautious, as children may eat many bright berries. The ASPCA page was blocked in this run, so there is no pet-specific source beyond Massey (dogs, livestock). Data note: the mapping has a misspelt species name 'Cotonoaster' (55 trees). It still matches because its Latin name is 'Cotoneaster'. Row also covers C. frigidus, C. frigidus salicifolius and C. salicifolius.

name: Box elder
edible: Box elder is a maple. Its sap can be tapped in late winter, when frosty nights are followed by milder days, and boiled down into syrup.
poisonous: Seeds contain hypoglycin A, which causes a muscle disease in horses (seasonal pasture or atypical myopathy). Most affected horses die. Keep horses away from fallen seeds.
research_notes: Replaced Wikipedia with Univ. Minnesota Extension and Cornell vet. The RVC page only names sycamore, not box elder, so it is not cited here. 'Not a risk to people' dropped (no source says it either way). Regex 'ash.leaved maple' won't match 'Ashleaf Maple' in the data; it is caught by 'acer negundo' instead. Suggest 'ash.?lea(f|ved) maple'.

name: Sycamore
edible: The sugary sap has been tapped and drunk in Britain and in other parts of Europe.
poisonous: The seeds and seedlings contain hypoglycin A. In horses this causes atypical myopathy, a muscle disease that kills about three in four affected horses. The risk peaks in autumn, when seeds fall on pasture, and in spring, when they sprout.
research_notes: Dropped the 'boiled down to a syrup' claim: only the Kent herbarium mentions syrup. The tree-sap review (Svanberg et al. 2012, Acta Soc Bot Pol) records fresh and fermented use but no syrup for sycamore. Dropped 'Not a risk to people': I found no source for it. The owner may know that hypoglycin A is the same toxin as in unripe ackee fruit, which poisons people. I did not research this, so the website should not claim people are safe. The BHS page was blocked when I tried to open it. Many sources about 'sycamore syrup' are about American sycamore (Platanus), a different tree, so don't cite them. Teagasc is the Irish state agriculture agency. PFAF pages served the wrong plant every time I tried them, so I did not use PFAF anywhere. | FACT-CHECK: edible reworded after independent check ('Early spring' is not in either source (the sap review gives no season for sycamore). 'Fermented into wine' rests on Kent herbarium only (review's table is uncl)

name: Maple
edible: The sap of any maple can be boiled down to syrup. Sugar maple has the sweetest sap, so it is the main syrup tree. Trees are tapped in late winter, before the buds open. No other maple part is reliably documented as food.
poisonous: Wilted or dried leaves of red maple, from fallen or cut branches, are very dangerous to horses and ponies. They destroy red blood cells, and horses can die within a day. Fresh leaves do not seem to cause this. No known risk to people.
research_notes: This row covers Norway, field, silver, sugar, red, Cappadocian, Japanese (A. japonicum, A. palmatum), snakebark, paperbark and Montpellier maples. Edible: Ohio State says 'all maples will produce sap that can be boiled to make syrup' and that sugar maple is sweetest. Utah State says sap can be harvested from any maple and gives late winter until bud swell as the season. Woodland Trust says the same for field maple. 'Late winter' has two sources (Ohio State: February; Utah State: mid-late Feb until bud swell). The last sentence of the edible note is my own summary that nothing else could be sourced. Dropped the claim about eating young boiled seeds: no second reputable source found. Poisonous: the red maple horse claim has two sources (Ontario ministry, Tufts vet school). Ontario notes the suspect chemical (gallic acid) is also in silver and sugar maple but with no published poisoning cases, so I left that out. 'No known risk to people' reflects that no source I read reports any; delete it if you want strictly positive claims. Horse owners should also see the separate sycamore and box elder rows (atypical myopathy). Regex: 'acer' also matches Acer pseudoplatanus (sycamore) and Acer negundo (box elder). The mapping shows them going to their own rows, so make sure those rows are matched first. Woodland Trust mentions Culpeper's liver remedy, but that is a single historical source, so medicinal is left empty.

name: Rowan
edible: The berries are bitter and should not be eaten raw. Raw berries contain parasorbic acid, which cooking breaks down. Cooked, they make a sharp jelly or jam.
research_notes: Dropped the freezing claim: only Wisconsin mentions it, and says freezing helps 'to a lesser extent'. Dropped 'with apples' (only the Woodland Trust recipe; it uses crab apples/Bramley cores for pectin). Wisconsin also says seeds probably contain cyanide-releasing compounds ('probably', one source) - not included. Row also catches Japanese rowan (Sorbus commixta, 8 trees) and Vilmorin's rowan (S. vilmorinii, 1 tree); none of the sources cover these, so the notes are only verified for S. aucuparia. Suggest splitting: keep 'Rowan' regex as 'rowan(?!.*(japanese|vilmorin))|mountain ash|aucuparia' or add a row 'Other rowans' (Sorbus commixta, Sorbus vilmorinii) with empty notes. The Wisconsin page needed a second attempt to open (first was blocked by a permission timeout) and was opened successfully.

name: Whitebeam
edible: The red berries are edible once bletted, meaning left until very soft and nearly rotten. In northern and central Europe they were also dried and ground into a flour to stretch bread.
research_notes: Dropped 'cooked into jelly' (only PFAF says 'preserves'). Dropped PFAF's mild diuretic/laxative medicinal claim (single source). PFAF says the seeds probably contain cyanogenic compounds (single source, dropped). Swedish whitebeam (S. intermedia) and broad-leaved whitebeam (S. latifolia) are edible raw or cooked per PFAF only; I found no second source for those species. Woodland Trust says 'edible when nearly rotten' (chess apples). Regex: 'intermedia' will also match unrelated plants such as Hamamelis x intermedia (witch hazel) or Forsythia x intermedia; suggest 'sorbus intermedia'. 'swedish' alone could catch other 'Swedish' cultivars; suggest 'swedish whitebeam'.

name: Service tree
edible: Fruits of both service trees are very sharp and astringent when picked. Once bletted (left to over-ripen, or softened by frost) they turn soft and sweet and can be eaten raw. Wild service fruits are known as chequers. Both kinds were also made into alcoholic drinks.
medicinal: The fruit was a traditional remedy for colic and other bowel complaints. This is historical folk use, not a modern treatment.
research_notes: Dropped single-source claims: 'taste like dates' (Woodland Trust only), 'flavoured beer' (Oxford Botanic Garden; PFAF only via a reader comment), and the meaning of 'torminalis' = colic (Oxford only). Medicinal support for colic is Oxford Botanic Garden (two species pages, same institution) plus PFAF; it's thin, so consider dropping the medicinal note. PFAF says the seeds 'probably' contain cyanide-forming compounds; unsupported elsewhere so no poisonous note. Latin: S. torminalis is now often treated as Torminalis glaberrima (RHS) and S. domestica as Cormus domestica.

name: Rowan / whitebeam family
edible: The berries are not eaten raw. Rowan berries are bitter and sour raw and can upset the stomach; they are cooked, usually into a jelly. Whitebeam and wild service fruits are eaten only when bletted: left until soft and nearly rotten.
research_notes: In species-mapping.txt no species currently falls under this row: Rowan, Whitebeam and Service tree rows catch all Sorbus first, so this is a fallback only; consider deleting it. Rowan raw-berry claims are well sourced (Wisconsin uncommon fruit, Woodland Trust, Wild Food UK, pfaf; parasorbic acid, which heat breaks down). Bletting for whitebeam and wild service rests on one Woodland Trust page each (same organisation) - weaker. No sources found for Swedish whitebeam, Japanese rowan or Vilmorin's rowan. Seeds 'probably contain hydrogen cyanide' (Wisconsin, pfaf) - hedged in both, so not added. pfaf medicinal uses not added (single source).

name: Pear
edible: Common pears ripen from late summer into autumn. They are picked while still firm and ripened indoors, then eaten raw or cooked, for example in pies. Many street pears are ornamental kinds, such as Callery pear, with marble-sized, hard brown fruit that only softens after frost. Birds eat these.
research_notes: The biggest group in this row is 'Pyrus' unspecified (1,263 trees), probably mostly ornamental Callery pears, plus Pyrus communis (202) and willow-leaved pear P. salicifolia (18). I dropped the old claim that Callery fruit 'sweetens once bletted' and is edible for people. Clemson and the Minnesota Dept of Agriculture confirm it softens after frost and birds eat it, but neither says people eat it, and the pfaf page was blocked. Also dropped the amygdalin-in-pips claim, as I could not open two sources in this run. I found no source on willow-leaved pear fruit. Consider splitting: 'Pear (fruiting)' (Pyrus communis) on the edible layer, and 'Ornamental pear' (Pyrus calleryana, Pyrus salicifolia, Pyrus spp.) off it.

name: Apple / crab apple
edible: Apples and crab apples are edible. Crab apples are very sour, so are mostly cooked: made into jelly, roasted with meat or added to drinks. They are rich in pectin, which helps jams set. Eat the flesh only and throw away the pips.
poisonous: Pips, leaves and stems contain compounds that release cyanide, and wilting leaves are the most toxic. Mainly a concern for dogs, cats and horses.
research_notes: Sources are about wild crab apple (M. sylvestris) and apple generally; I found nothing on fruit of ornamental crabs (M. floribunda, hupehensis, baccata, purpurea etc.) specifically. NC State says seeds are toxic only in large quantities (single source, so not stated). Owner may prefer to leave apple off the poisonous layer since the risk is mainly to animals. Regex: 'apple' would also match e.g. 'Pineapple', 'Thorn-apple' if they ever appear; '\bplum\b' in row 48 also matches 'Plum-leaved Apple' - currently fine only because Apple is tested first.

name: Medlar
edible: The fruit is picked in late autumn, after frost, while it is still hard and sour. It is then stored until it 'blets', meaning it softens and turns brown. This sweetens it. Only then is the soft flesh eaten, or made into jelly.
research_notes: Dropped the 'spiced apple purée' taste description: no second source. Only RHS says to throw away the skin and seeds, so that is left out.

name: Quince
edible: The fruit is hard, sour and astringent (mouth-drying) raw, so it is almost always cooked. It is rich in pectin, which makes it set well as jelly. It is also made into jam and a thick quince paste (membrillo).
research_notes: Claim-to-source map. Hard/sour/astringent raw, usually cooked: RHS ('aren't edible raw'), UC ANR, Springer review (Norbova et al. 2024), Iberian-American Fruits book chapter (Univ. Algarve repository). Jelly: RHS, UC ANR, Springer, book chapter. Pectin: UC ANR (only one source, but it explains the jelly use; delete 'rich in pectin' if you want strict two-source sourcing). Jam: RHS, Springer, book chapter. Membrillo/paste: RHS and book chapter ('marmelada'). Dropped harvest month (Oct-Nov, RHS only). Dropped the seed warning: the Springer review says the seeds can release cyanide, but I could not find a second reputable source. Worth adding if you find one. Medicinal left empty: two reviews describe traditional use (seeds and leaves for coughs, sore throats, diarrhoea) but neither gave a clear statement on human evidence I could cite. A 2021 PMC amygdalin review (PMC8069783) lists Cydonia as an amygdalin-containing species but gives no quince-specific risk, so it is not cited. Regex 'quince' would also catch 'Japanese quince' (Chaenomeles) if it ever appears; not in the current list.

name: Juneberry
edible: The small berries ripen in summer, turning from red to dark purple. They taste a bit like blueberries. They can be eaten raw or cooked in jam, pies and muffins.
research_notes: Dropped: 'one of the best street-tree fruits' (opinion), 'June' (sources say summer / 2-3 months after bloom; Illinois says Saskatoon ripens in July), 'almond' flavour (no source), 'seeds are fine in normal amounts' (no source opened says anything about the seeds' safety). Only RHS is specific to A. lamarckii; the extension pages cover serviceberries (Amelanchier) generally. Snowy mespilus (A. ovalis, 1 tree) is not specifically covered by any opened source. RHS notes it is grown as an ornamental in the UK rather than for fruit.

name: Strawberry tree
edible: The knobbly red fruits can be eaten raw but are rather bland, so they are rarely eaten fresh. Most are made into jam, jelly or strong spirits such as Portuguese medronho. The name 'unedo' is said to come from Latin for 'I eat one'.
medicinal: Leaves, fruit and root have been used in Mediterranean folk medicine as a diuretic and antiseptic, including for urinary complaints. Research so far is mostly in the lab or in animals, so there is no good evidence that it works in people.
research_notes: 'Bland' = PFAF 'sweet but insipid' and Molecules review 'taste not much appreciated'. Dropped 'eat in moderation' (PFAF only; MDPI notes slightly fermented fruit can upset digestion; reader comments on PFAF about overripe fruit causing drunkenness are anecdotal). Dropped folk use for high blood pressure (one review only). Trees and Shrubs Online is from the International Dendrology Society (not on the approved list; used only as an extra source). Hybrid strawberry tree (A. x andrachnoides) not specifically covered by sources.

name: Mulberry
edible: Ripe fruits are eaten raw or made into jam, pies and other cooking. Black mulberry has the best flavour; its fruit ripens in August and September and is ready when soft and dark.
medicinal: White mulberry leaf is used in traditional Chinese medicine, including for diabetes. Some trials suggest it can modestly lower blood sugar, but good human research is limited. This applies to white mulberry leaf, not the fruit.
research_notes: Dropped: 'unripe fruit and milky sap upset the stomach' - only NC State Extension supports it (Morus alba and Morus rubra pages, same organisation); worth re-adding if a second source is found. Dropped NCCIH-only safety notes (may add to effect of diabetes medicines; pregnancy safety unknown) - these are worth keeping if a second source turns up. ROW MIX: Paper mulberry (Broussonetia papyrifera) matches 'mulberry' but is a different genus; NC State gives no edible or medicinal use for it (only notes allergenic pollen). Suggest a separate row 'Paper mulberry' (Broussonetia papyrifera) with empty fields, or exclude it via the regex (e.g. match '\bmorus\b|(?<!paper )mulberry').

name: Fig
edible: Ripe figs are eaten raw or cooked, or dried.
poisonous: The milky sap from cut leaves and shoots contains psoralens. On skin in sunlight it can cause burning redness and blisters (phytophotodermatitis), leaving dark marks that may last months. Gardeners pruning figs on sunny days are most at risk.
research_notes: 'In good summers' timing dropped (no source). Sources: BMJ Case Reports 2021 (PMC7813380), Cureus 2023, Dermatology Online Journal 2023. Severe cases can be extensive (BMJ: tree surgeon), so 'low' is borderline; 'moderate' is defensible. Dermatology Online Journal says the fruit and its sap lack psoralens; pfaf says sap and half-ripe fruit are 'said to be poisonous' and sap is a serious eye irritant (single source, not added). ASPCA's 'fig' page lists toxicity to dogs, cats and horses but for Ficus benjamina, not F. carica, so not used. pfaf medicinal uses not added (single source).

name: Persimmon
edible: Astringent kinds (such as 'Hachiya') are only pleasant once fully soft; firm fruit is mouth-puckering because of tannins. Non-astringent kinds (such as 'Fuyu') can be eaten firm. Eaten fresh or dried. Eating lots of persimmons often has been linked to hard lumps in the stomach (bezoars) that may need removing.
research_notes: species-mapping.txt lists NO persimmon or Diospyros trees, so this row currently shows on no trees. Consider removing it, or keep it for future data. Both ripeness sources are separate peer-reviewed University of Florida IFAS EDIS papers (different authors and topics). They're from one institution, so add an independent second source (e.g. RHS) if you want strict independence. The bezoar claim is supported by MSD Manual (professional) and a PMC case report and review. The date-plum (D. lotus) in the regex was not researched.

name: Loquat
edible: The flesh of ripe fruit is edible raw or made into jam or jelly. Do not eat the seeds.
poisonous: Seeds contain amygdalin, which turns into cyanide in the body. Eating them, especially as ground seed powder, can cause headache, dizziness, nausea and vomiting.
research_notes: Sources are Japan's agriculture ministry (MAFF, page in Japanese), Tokyo Metropolitan Government food-safety FAQ, and NC State. Dropped (single source): unripe fruit is also high in amygdalin (MAFF), spring fruiting and rarely fruiting in cold climates (NC State). Medicinal left empty: NC State only says 'historically used medicinally'.

name: Olive
edible: Raw olives are far too bitter to eat, even when ripe. They must be cured first, for example in water, brine or lye, which removes the bitter compounds.
medicinal: Olive leaf extract is sold as a supplement, mainly for blood pressure and heart health. Reviews of the trials suggest it may lower blood pressure slightly, but there are only a few small studies, so the evidence is weak.
research_notes: Dropped 'London trees rarely ripen fruit': I found no source. The two medicinal sources are meta-analyses (PeerJ 2021, 5 trials; Diabetol Metab Syndr 2022, 12 trials rated low to very low certainty for several outcomes). Lye is caustic. If you'd rather not name it on a family-facing site, 'water or brine' is enough.

name: Cornelian cherry
edible: The bright red fruits ripen in late summer, around August and September. They are tart, somewhere between cranberry and sour cherry. They are traditionally made into jam, preserves, juice and liqueurs.
medicinal: The fruit and leaves have been folk remedies for centuries. Lab and animal studies are promising, but there are very few human trials, so there is no good evidence that it treats any illness.
research_notes: Claim-to-source map. Bright red, late summer: Clemson ('late summer to early fall', 'bright-red') and Univ. Washington Botanic Gardens ('August and September'). Tart: Wisconsin ('very tart') and UW ('between cranberry and sour cherry'; the comparison itself is UW only). Jam/preserves: Clemson, UW, Wisconsin, Springer, Frontiers. Juice: Frontiers and Wisconsin (syrup). Liqueurs: UW, Springer ('liquors'), Frontiers ('alcoholic beverages'). Medicinal: traditional use from Frontiers (Czerwinska & Melzig 2018), Springer (Przeor et al. 2019) and Wisconsin. Thin human evidence: Frontiers ('no convincing human studies'; one small trial in children needs larger trials) and Springer (mostly in vitro and animal work). Dropped 'sour-sweet when soft' and the clinging stone (Wisconsin only). RHS Cornus mas page was blocked for this run.

name: Cherry plum
edible: Small red, orange or yellow plums follow the early spring blossom. They can be eaten raw or made into jam, jelly or tarts. Do not crack or chew the stones: the kernels inside contain compounds that release cyanide.
research_notes: Dropped 'July and August' and 'first wild fruit of summer' (no source gives ripening months; RHS lists fruit colour under autumn). Stone warning: NC State (pits contain cyanide compounds; crushing/chewing raises risk) + PMC review (plum kernels contain amygdalin, which releases hydrogen cyanide). NC State also lists leaves and stems as poisonous (medium severity) - single source, so not added; owner could consider a poisonous entry if a second source is found. Most map trees are the purple-leaved var. pissardii; RHS says the species fruits only sometimes, and no source specific to pissardii fruit was opened.

name: Blackthorn
edible: The dark sloes are very sour and drying in the mouth when raw. They are picked in autumn, traditionally after a frost which softens the taste, and used for sloe gin, jams and jellies. Do not crack or eat the stones, which contain compounds that can release cyanide.
medicinal: Bark, flowers, leaves and fruit were used in folk medicine, mainly as a mild laxative and for stomach complaints. Modern studies have only been done in the lab or on animals, with no trials in people.
research_notes: The 'after a frost' claim rests on Wild Food UK plus PFAF (both 'one-of-two' sources); owner may want to drop it. Stones: Zurich vet toxicology database (seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides, species rated weakly toxic; fruit flesh has practically none) plus PFAF. Blackthorn left off the poisonous layer because only the stones are a (weak) concern. 'Laxative' supported by the Molecules 2023 review and PFAF; 'digestive complaints' by Woodland Trust. Woodland Trust also warns thorns can break off in skin and cause infection (single source, not used).

name: Bird cherry
medicinal: The bark was a folk remedy for coughs, colds and other ailments. This is historical use only.
poisonous: Leaves, stems and seeds (inside the stones) contain substances that release cyanide. The leaves are toxic to grazing animals, and dogs, cats and horses can be poisoned. People should not chew or eat the stones.
research_notes: Edible left empty: both sources call the fruit bitter, but uses differ (Woodland Trust: liqueur flavouring; PFAF: jams/preserves) and each is single-sourced. Could restore 'bitter fruit used in preserves' with a second source. ASPCA page is for Prunus spp. generally. Medicinal is thin (folk use only); consider dropping. Woodland Trust names goats specifically as at risk (single source).

name: Wild cherry
edible: The small red to dark cherries ripen in summer and can be eaten raw or cooked; birds take many. Do not crack, chew or blend the stones: the kernels are toxic.
poisonous: Stones (kernels), leaves and fruit stalks contain cyanogenic glycosides, which release cyanide. Crushed kernels are the main risk to people. Leaves and stones are poisonous to dogs, cats and horses.
research_notes: Medicinal dropped: the original 'wild cherry bark in cough syrups' refers to American black cherry (Prunus serotina), not P. avium. Woodland Trust and pfaf both mention the trunk resin as an old cough remedy, but there is no evidence statement and it is minor folk use, so left empty. 'Sour' and 'birds get most' softened to sourced wording. NC State: swallowing a couple of whole stones should not poison (single source, not added). pfaf contradicts itself by listing the seed as edible while warning of cyanide - ignored. 'Wild Cherry Double Gean' (Prunus avium 'Plena') bears little or no fruit (not sourced). NC State rates severity 'medium'. ASPCA page covers Prunus spp.

name: Almond
poisonous: Bitter almond kernels contain amygdalin, which turns into cyanide in the body. Cyanide poisoning causes nausea, headache and weakness, and can kill. Young children are most at risk: only a few bitter kernels could be fatal.
research_notes: Risk raised from moderate to high: FSA/FSS say cyanide can be fatal, and India's FSSAI says 5 to 10 bitter almonds could kill a young child (the number is left out of the note on purpose). A PubMed case report, 'Child cyanide poisoning after ingestion of bitter almonds' (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20560788/), was opened but has no abstract, so it is not cited. Weak point: that sweet almonds are 'the usual food nut' with almost no amygdalin rests mainly on one peer-reviewed paper (PMC8831915: common almond has almost undetectable amygdalin). The RHS almond page was blocked in this run. Street almond trees are often ornamental, and their kernels may be bitter. Regex note: 'almond' would also match any 'Dwarf Russian almond' or 'Flowering almond' entries (none in the mapping now). | FACT-CHECK: edible note removed: a street almond may be bitter, and tasting to check is unsafe.

name: Plum, peach and apricot
edible: Plums, gages and damsons ripen from late summer into autumn. They can be eaten fresh or cooked into jams and puddings; damsons are mostly cooked. Never crack or eat the stones.
poisonous: The kernels inside the stones contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide. Crushing or chewing them makes this worse. It can cause headache, dizziness and vomiting. Leaves, stems and kernels are also a risk to dogs, cats and horses.
research_notes: Peach fruit being edible raw or cooked is in NC State only (RHS peach page could not be opened), so the edible note names plums/gages/damsons; owner may add peaches. MAFF covers apricot, plum and peach kernels; it also reports deaths abroad from raw apricot kernels (single source). NC State rates peach 'medium' severity, hence moderate. The Tokyo page is about loquat seeds but describes amygdalin symptoms generally. REGEX: '\bplum\b' also matches 'Cherry Plum' and 'Plum-leaved Apple' - currently fine only because those rows are tested first; safer to use '^plum\b|wild plum|prunus domestica'.

name: Ornamental cherry
poisonous: The leaves, twigs and the seeds inside the stones contain compounds that release cyanide. Wilting leaves, for example on fallen or cut branches, are the most dangerous. The main risk is to dogs, cats, horses and grazing livestock.
research_notes: ROW SHOULD BE SPLIT. It mixes generic 'Cherry' (Prunus, 4801 trees, which may include wild cherry and plums), P. serrulata, P. maackii, P. incisa, and two cherries with edible fruit: Dwarf Cherry P. cerasus (sour cherry) and Rum Cherry P. serotina (black cherry). No edible note can be true for all of them, so I left edible empty. The old sakura blossom/leaf claim fits only Japanese flowering cherries and had a single (PFAF) source. Suggested new rows: 'Sour cherry' (Prunus cerasus, match 'dwarf cherry|sour cherry|morello|prunus cerasus') and 'Black cherry' (Prunus serotina, match 'rum cherry|black cherry|prunus serotina'). NC State calls black cherry fruit bitter but usable for jam. It also says the fruit, leaves and seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides and can kill livestock. Research both new rows separately. Also check that the bare 'cherry|prunus' match runs after the Cherry laurel, Bird cherry, Wild cherry, Cherry plum, Blackthorn, Almond and Plum rows. The mapping suggests it does today. The poisonous note is written for the whole genus: ASPCA covers Prunus spp. I rated it low because the sources are about animals; none of the four I opened gives human poisoning cases. NC State says swallowing a couple of whole stones won't poison a person (single source, so left out).

name: Sea buckthorn
edible: The orange berries are made into juice, jams and syrups. They are very rich in vitamin C.
medicinal: Berries, leaves and oil have long been used in traditional medicine in Tibet, China and Central Asia, for skin and digestive problems among others. A few small human trials (for example burns, dry eyes) look hopeful, but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. It did not help colds or eczema.
research_notes: Claim-to-source map. Juice/jams/syrups: PMC9366820 (Zuchowski 2022, Phytochemistry Reviews), PMC9763470 (Frontiers in Nutrition 2022), and Univ. Michigan Health library (juice, puree). Vitamin C: both PMC reviews. Traditional use in Tibet/China/Central Asia: PMC9366820, PMC9763470 (Tibetan medical classic) and UMich ('central and eastern Asia'). Skin and digestive uses: UMich and PMC9763470. Mostly lab/animal evidence: both PMC reviews. Small trials on burns and dry eye: UMich and PMC9763470 (burns). 'Did not help colds or eczema' is UMich only; cut it for strict two-source sourcing. Dropped 'very sour' (no source I opened describes the taste). Dropped UMich's warning that the berry oil reduces platelet activity, so people on blood thinners should take advice: only one source. Worth restoring if you find a second. Univ. Michigan Health's library is Healthwise-authored consumer content; swap it if you want stricter sources.

name: Buckthorn
medicinal: The dried bark of alder buckthorn is a strong stimulant laxative. European regulators accept it for short-term relief of occasional constipation, based on long use. Purging buckthorn berries were once used as a purge. Avoid when breastfeeding, as it can give the baby loose stools.
poisonous: The dark berries of both purging and alder buckthorn are mildly poisonous. They act as a strong laxative and can cause sickness, vomiting and diarrhoea.
research_notes: NO TREES IN THE MAP fall under this row (species-mapping.txt has no Rhamnus or Frangula). REGEX PROBLEM: 'buckthorn' matches 'Sea-buckthorn' and 'rhamnus' matches 'Hippophae rhamnoides'; sea buckthorn currently lands in its own row only because of row order. Suggest '\bbuckthorn' with a negative check for 'sea', and 'rhamnus\b' instead of 'rhamnus'. Latin: row covers two species, suggest latin 'Rhamnus cathartica / Frangula alnus'. Risk changed from moderate to low: NC State rates both 'low severity' and the Woodland Trust says 'slightly poisonous'. EMA also says not for children under 12, not in pregnancy, and no longer than one week - only one source (EMA) for these, so dropped; the EMA well-established-use statement itself is single-source but the laxative action is backed by LactMed (NIH) and Woodland Trust. Dropped 'now little used because of side effects' (no source). LactMed warns not to confuse these with sea buckthorn.

name: Hawthorn
edible: Young leaves, flower buds and flowers can be eaten raw in spring salads. The red haws (berries) can be eaten raw but are better cooked into jelly and other preserves.
medicinal: Leaves and flowers are a traditional herbal remedy for the heart. Trials in heart failure have mixed results: some found it eased symptoms, others found no benefit. It may interact with heart medicines and must not replace them, so talk to a doctor first. Not recommended in pregnancy.
research_notes: Round 2: medicinal rewritten so each claim has two sources: American Family Physician review (2010; mixed trials, no reduction in deaths, possible interactions with digoxin and blood-pressure drugs, don't replace standard care) and Memorial Sloan Kettering herb page (mixed evidence, digoxin interaction, use only under a doctor). EMA kept as support for traditional heart use. EMA's 'mild nervous palpitations, traditional use only' detail dropped (single source). Both AAFP and MSKCC say avoid in pregnancy - could be added if wanted. NCCIH and MedlinePlus still not reachable. Edible kept from round 1. Earlier notes still apply: edibility sources are for C. monogyna only (row also covers Midland hawthorn and cockspur thorns); check '\bmay\b' regex; 'bread and cheese', ketchup and seed-cyanide claims dropped as single-sourced. | FACT-CHECK: medicinal reworded after independent check (Missing warning given by two sources: AAFP and MSKCC both say not to use in pregnancy. 'Show no fewer deaths' is AAFP only (MSKCC gives no mortality data). 'Ber)

name: Elder
edible: The flowers are used for cordial, tea, wine and fritters. Ripe black berries are cooked into jams, pies, syrups and wine. Always cook the berries; the rest of the plant is not edible.
medicinal: Elderflower is a traditional remedy for the early symptoms of colds and for chest complaints. European regulators accept it on the basis of long use, but there are few clinical studies to show it works.
poisonous: Leaves, stems, roots and seeds contain substances that release cyanide, and raw berries can upset the stomach. Eating them can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Cooking makes ripe berries safe to eat.
research_notes: Round 2: no change. Round-1 fields kept (properly sourced). Tried again to source an elderBERRY cold/flu evidence line: NCCIH (european-elder) was blocked and MedlinePlus herb pages fail at the site, so the medicinal note stays on elderflower (EMA + pfaf). EMA restricts elderflower medicines to over-12s (single source, not included). 'Strip the stalks' and 'unripe berries' wording still unsourced.

name: Pagoda tree
medicinal: The flower buds are used in traditional Chinese and other Asian medicine, for example to stop bleeding. These are traditional uses, not proven treatments. Not for use in pregnancy.
poisonous: The pods and seeds are poisonous. Eating them can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and, in larger amounts, agitation or drowsiness. Children are most at risk because the pods are easy to pick up.
