research_notes: WEAK ROW: pfaf is one of only two sources for each field. Medicinal: NC State says buds are used in Asia as an astringent; pfaf says TCM, haemostatic, and 'should not be prescribed for pregnant women' (pregnancy warning is pfaf only - consider removing). 'Commercial source of rutin' dropped (pfaf only). The 'not proven' sentence has no explicit source; neither source cites clinical evidence. Poison: NC State lists vomiting, diarrhoea, excitability, delirium, coma and rates severity LOW and flags children; pfaf says it contains cytisine, 'similarly toxic' to nicotine. I kept 'moderate' (likely to make a person ill); owner may prefer 'low' per NC State. 'Cytisine-like alkaloids' wording replaced (NC State only says 'possibly alkaloids'). Edible left empty: NC State and pfaf say young leaves and flowers are edible (pfaf: cooked, in several changes of water), but this is marginal and sits badly next to toxic pods for a family audience.

name: Wisteria
poisonous: All parts contain toxins, but the bean-like seed pods and seeds are the most dangerous and the parts most often swallowed. Eating them can cause a burning mouth, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Seek medical help if any is swallowed.
research_notes: Round 2: poisonous restored. Sources: Poison Control (US national capital poison center), Queensland Children's Health (W. floribunda page; same toxins), NC State (lists all parts toxic, symptoms vomiting/diarrhoea; flags dogs, cats and horses). Edible DROPPED because sources conflict: NC State says flowers are edible raw or cooked, but Poison Control says all parts including flowers contain the toxins and twins who ate flowers, pods and seeds were hospitalised. Not safe to put wisteria on the edible layer. ASPCA page was blocked. NC State rates severity low; poison centres describe hospital treatment and possible collapse, hence moderate.

name: Japanese knotweed
edible: Young spring shoots are edible cooked, with a sour, rhubarb-like taste. Don't pick it here: it is often treated with weedkiller, and it is an offence to cause it to grow in the wild, which tiny pieces of root or stem can do.
medicinal: The root is a traditional Chinese medicine called huzhang, and contains resveratrol. Research is mostly in cells and animals, so benefits in people are not proven. Don't self-treat.
research_notes: Sources by claim: shoots edible/rhubarb taste = NC State + PFAF (PFAF adds 'cooked'; NC State just says young stems edible). Weedkiller = GOV.UK + NRW + RHS (all describe herbicide control; 'often treated' is a fair summary, not a claim about councils specifically). Offence to cause it to grow in the wild = RHS + NRW (Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 Sch. 9); GOV.UK says you can be prosecuted for causing it to spread; GOV.UK + NRW support spread from small fragments. Medicinal: huzhang root use, resveratrol in rhizome, and mainly cell/animal evidence = two peer-reviewed reviews (PMC9833411, Frontiers 2022). Dropped (single source): 'major commercial source of resveratrol' (neither review says so); reported kidney toxicity (PMC review only); PFAF oxalic acid caution. Accepted name is Reynoutria japonica.

name: Kousa dogwood
edible: The round pink-red fruits are edible when ripe. Edible dogwood fruits like these are eaten in parts of Asia and Europe.
research_notes: Kept deliberately short. These details each had only one source and were left out: 'raspberry-like / custardy', 'skip the bitter skin' (no source), 'sweet' (Foods 2022 review only), 'hard stone' and 'mostly left for birds' (NC State only), and 'made into wine' (Foods review only). One more source could restore a sweet-flesh/stone description. Only 2 trees on the map.

name: Firethorn
poisonous: The berries are not considered seriously poisonous, but eating a lot can cause a mild stomach upset such as sickness. The sharp thorns can cause wounds and skin irritation.
research_notes: Berries: poison.org (US National Capital Poison Center) says not considered poisonous, large amounts may cause mild nausea/vomiting, tiny amounts of a cyanide-like compound; CHOP Poison Control lists pyracantha as non-poisonous 'unless large amounts are eaten' and says thorns can cause an irritating rash; Utah Poison Control says possible skin and stomach irritant. Edible field left empty: CHOP only says 'some sources report them to be edible' and poison.org says there are no recommendations to eat them, so the old jelly note is not supported. ASPCA page blocked (permission timeout). Pets: poison.org cites a study where animals ate large amounts without signs of toxicity - single source, not added. Risk 'low' means mild for people; owner may prefer to keep this row off the poisonous layer altogether. Covers P. coccinea and P. atalantoides.

name: Lilac
edible: The flowers of common lilac can be eaten raw or dipped in batter and fried as fritters. The flowers are the only part listed as edible.
research_notes: Round 2. Edible sourced from NC State Extension and PFAF (both: flowers raw or in fritters). 'Floral, slightly bitter' taste and use in syrups/sugars dropped (no two sources; Wild Food UK blocked). 'Flowers are the only part listed as edible' is PFAF's wording; NC State lists only flowers as edible too. No medicinal use with two sources (PFAF only). Neither source lists toxicity. The 2 genus-only 'Syringa' trees fall under this row; the note is about Syringa vulgaris, so other lilac species are not covered.

name: Hibiscus
edible: The flowers of this hardy garden hibiscus (rose of Sharon) are edible.
research_notes: Dropped young leaves and tea (PFAF only; NC State confirms flowers only). Dropped PFAF folk medicinal uses (single source). NC State tags it non-toxic to cats, dogs and horses. 19 map trees are just 'Hibiscus' with no species; outdoors in London these are almost certainly H. syriacus, but the note is only sourced for that species.

name: Japanese angelica tree
edible: Young spring shoots are eaten cooked, for example blanched, as a wild vegetable in Japan and Korea. The stems, trunk and leaf stalks carry sharp spines.
medicinal: Used in East Asian folk medicine, for example for diabetes and rheumatism. Lab research is ongoing, but benefits in people are not proven.
research_notes: Edible: PFAF says young shoots cooked/blanched; PubMed review (Food Chem/2021 review 'A Review on a Medicinal and Edible Plant: Aralia elata') calls it a prized wild vegetable in China, Japan, Korea and Russia; Springer (Hortic. Environ. Biotechnol. 2022) includes A. elata among Korean spring sprouts that are 'usually blanched and eaten'; encyclopedia.pub entry (MDPI community encyclopedia - borderline reputable) gives shoots blanched/pickled/deep-fried in Korea and Japan and warns the attached woody stem has sharp thorns. Spines: NC State + encyclopedia.pub. 'Tempura' and 'taranome' names not stated (not two sources). Medicinal: PubMed review (folk use for diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis; effects 'still need to be proven') + PFAF (rheumatoid arthralgia, diabetes). The 'not proven' clause rests mainly on the review; owner may prefer to leave medicinal empty for a 1-tree row.

name: Nettle tree
research_notes: Edible note removed: only pfaf supports it (fruit raw, small, mostly stone, 'mealy pleasant' or 'insipidly sweet', seeds ripen October). I could not open a second source (NC State page failed; RHS and JRC atlas pages were blocked). If a second source is found, restore something like 'small dark fruits, mostly stone, eaten raw; sweet but thin'. pfaf medicinal uses (astringent leaves/fruit) are single-source. No toxicity found.

name: Ginkgo
edible: The seed inside the smelly fruit can be eaten after the pulp is removed and the seed is boiled or roasted. Eat only a few: large amounts are poisonous, even when cooked. Never eat raw seeds or the fleshy pulp.
medicinal: Leaf extract is a popular supplement taken for memory. A large US trial of over 3,000 older people found it did not prevent dementia or Alzheimer's. Bleeding has been reported, so anyone on blood thinners should check with a doctor first.
poisonous: The seeds, especially raw ones, contain a toxin that blocks vitamin B6. Eating too many can cause vomiting and seizures. Juice from the fruit pulp can irritate the skin, so handle fallen fruit with gloves.
research_notes: Round 2: all three fields restored from opened sources. Medicinal: 'did not prevent dementia' rests on two NIH news releases about the same GEM trial (nih.gov/node/24516 and node/8756); NCCIH, MedlinePlus, PubMed GEM abstract and PMC pages were blocked or failed. Note the NIH release found no extra bleeding in GEM; the bleeding line is from EMA (bleeding reported; consult doctor if on blood thinners) plus pfaf (avoid with warfarin). EMA accepts ginkgo dry extract for mild age-related dementia symptoms (single source, not included). Poisonous: 'deaths reported' is from the Hong Kong Hospital Authority poisonous-plant atlas; 'especially raw' from HA HK and pfaf (cooking reduces but pfaf/HA do not say cooked seeds are safe). 'Children more at risk' dropped (pfaf only). NC State rates severity low; HA HK reports fatalities - I chose moderate. Fatal cases (HA HK only) left out of the note. | FACT-CHECK: edible reworded after independent check ('Eaten in East Asia' is not stated in either cited source. Pulp removal + boiling/roasting is NC State; heating is pfaf. Safety: cooked seeds can still poison i) | FACT-CHECK: risk raised to high after independent check: deaths are reported.

name: False acacia (Robinia)
edible: Only the white flowers are eaten. Every other part, especially the bark and seeds, is poisonous.
poisonous: Bark, seeds and leaves are poisonous; the flowers are not. Eating them causes sickness, vomiting, weakness and tiredness, and large amounts can cause fits, coma and death. Children have been made ill by chewing the bark. Horses are especially at risk; cattle, sheep and poultry have also been poisoned.
research_notes: ROUND 2: risk raised to HIGH: NC State rates severity high ('may cause death in humans and livestock and pets') and poison.org (US poison centre) says large amounts can cause paralysis, coma and seizures. Children: poison.org and a PubMed case report (8-year-old ill after chewing bark; human cases rare). Horses most susceptible: Texas A&M Range Plants ('horses are most often poisoned') and Cornell. Flowers: NC State 'edible', poison.org 'nontoxic or much less toxic', PFAF cooked. 'Cooked'/'fritters' (PFAF only) not added. DISAGREEMENT: PFAF lists cooked seeds as edible; NC State and poison.org list seeds as poisonous - cautious view kept. 'Fritters' and PFAF medicinal uses dropped (single source). ASPCA black-locust page and PMC11728309 (horse case report) were blocked.

name: Honey locust
edible: The pods are edible: the pulp inside can be eaten raw or cooked. It is a minor food, though, and the pods are mostly eaten by farm animals and wildlife.
research_notes: Round 2: edible filled with NC State (pulp edible raw or cooked, mostly eaten by livestock and wildlife) and USDA FEIS (pods edible; eaten by cattle, goats, deer). 'Sweet' dropped: FEIS does not describe taste (NC State notes Native Americans used the dried pulp as a sweetener - single source). Many street trees are thornless, mostly podless cultivars such as 'Sunburst' (not double-sourced, so not in the note). NC State tags it non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses. Note: honey locust is a weak edible-layer candidate; owner may prefer to drop it.

name: Stag's horn sumach
edible: The red, hairy fruit clusters can be soaked in water to make a tart, lemony drink.
research_notes: Drink supported by NC State Extension and USDA Forest Service 'Plant of the Week' (both opened). NC State also says the plant 'is not poisonous' - single source, so not stated. Old spice claim not restored: the culinary spice sumac is usually Rhus coriaria, not checked against two sources. FEIS page failed to load. Regex 'rhus' fine.

name: Sweet gum
medicinal: Native American peoples used the gummy resin and inner bark as folk medicine, taken for diarrhoea and dysentery and put on wounds and skin sores. The hardened resin was also chewed like gum. These are traditional uses only; they have not been shown to work.
research_notes: Round 2. Medicinal sourced from University of Kentucky Urban Forest Initiative (diarrhoea, wounds/skin, resin chewed as gum), NC State (folk medicine for dysentery and diarrhoea; chewing gum), PFAF (dysentery, wounds, sores) and a University of Vermont library exhibit (wounds, coughs, diarrhoea; uncited, used only as extra support). 'Have not been shown to work' reflects that none of the sources reports any clinical evidence; NC State presents them only as folk uses. Dropped: friar's balsam and coughs (PFAF only). As round 1 suspected, 'storax' is mainly linked to Oriental sweetgum (Liquidambar orientalis) per the Kentucky page, so do not call this tree's resin storax. Chewing the resin was not put on the edible layer as it is not really food. USDA plant guide (plants.usda.gov) was blocked. No toxicity found (NC State silent, PFAF 'none known').

name: Tupelo
edible: The fruits are edible but very sour. They can be eaten raw or cooked into preserves.
research_notes: Suggested latin: Nyssa sylvatica (black tupelo / black gum); all 4 map trees are this species. The edible claim is sourced twice but is marginal for the 'genuinely eaten in practice' test (fruit is small, mainly eaten by birds per NC State); owner may prefer to leave this row off the edible layer. Native American medicinal uses of the bark (worms, emetic) are in PFAF only, so dropped. No toxicity found.

name: Eucalyptus
medicinal: Oil from the leaves is a traditional remedy for coughs and colds, breathed in with steam or rubbed on the skin, and is in many cold products. European regulators accept it on the basis of long use rather than strong trial evidence. Do not use it on babies or toddlers.
poisonous: The danger is the concentrated oil made from the leaves, not the tree. Swallowing even a small amount of oil can cause vomiting, drowsiness and seizures, and can be fatal. Young children are most at risk, so keep oil products out of reach.
research_notes: Round 2: poisonous note restored from Poison Control (teaspoon or less of undiluted oil can be fatal; seizures; under-2s should not be given it), Health Canada (seizures if swallowed by children) and MedlinePlus (symptoms incl. seizures, drowsiness, vomiting). Risk kept at moderate because the hazard is a manufactured oil, not the tree; you could argue high. Medicinal kept from round 1 (EMA + pfaf). RCH and HealthyWA still not opened. REGEX note from round 1 still applies: '\bgum\b' also matches Sweet Gum; keep Sweet gum row before Eucalyptus. | FACT-CHECK: medicinal reworded after independent check (Missing child-safety warning that two sources give: EMA says these medicines must not be used in children under 30 months (risk of laryngeal spasm) or children ) | FACT-CHECK: risk raised to high after independent check: deaths are reported.

name: Judas tree
edible: The pink flowers can be eaten raw, for example in salads. They have a sweet but sharp taste.
research_notes: 'Pea-like' taste dropped (unsourced). NC State calls the sweet-acid taste 'purported'. Pickled buds and raw pods are pfaf only, not added. Neither source lists toxicity. One map entry is genus 'Cercis' - redbud flowers are also widely eaten but not checked here.

name: Magnolia
research_notes: Round 2: left empty on purpose. The only reputable source found for edible magnolia flowers is pfaf for M. kobus (flowers and buds cooked; leaves for tea), and pfaf cannot be used alone. Search results for magnolia petals were only recipe blogs and shops. Wild Food UK's magnolia page was blocked. The gingery-petal claim also may not hold for every magnolia in this row (277 unspecified Magnolia, 5 M. acuminata). Recommend keeping Magnolia off the edible layer. pfaf lists no known hazards for M. kobus; ASPCA was not opened this round. No medicinal use found for these species (houpu bark is M. officinalis, not mapped). Suggest latin 'Magnolia' rather than 'Magnolia kobus'.

name: Ash
edible: Young, green, unripe keys (seeds) are edible.
medicinal: Ash leaf is a traditional herbal remedy for minor joint pain and to increase urine flow. EU regulators accept it on long-standing use alone, not proof from trials. It is not recommended in pregnancy, for under-18s, or for people with serious heart or kidney disease.
research_notes: 'Pickled as a caper substitute' dropped: PFAF says pickled, Woodland Trust only says edible; neither mentions capers. The 'accepted on tradition only' status and the pregnancy/under-18/heart-kidney warnings come from the EMA monograph alone (EMA overview page confirms the joint pain and urinary uses; PFAF confirms mild diuretic). EMA covers F. excelsior and F. angustifolia leaf only, not F. ornus/americana/velutina. PFAF says 'poisonous to ruminants' and occasional dermatitis, disputed in its own comments - not used. Manna ash (F. ornus) is the source of 'manna', a traditional laxative - not researched; could be its own row.

name: Southern beech
research_notes: Not researched: my web-search allowance ran out first. To my knowledge none of the four Nothofagus on the map (N. antarctica, N. obliqua, N. alpina, unnamed Nothofagus) has a meaningful edible, medicinal or poisonous use. That is unverified, so all fields stay empty. Suggested latin: 'Nothofagus spp.' (6+2+1+1 trees). Consider dropping this row from the layers if it stays empty.

name: Beech
edible: Very young, fresh spring leaves can be eaten. Beechnuts are eaten once cooked or roasted; they have also been roasted as a coffee substitute.
research_notes: Claim-to-source map. Young leaves: NC State ('young leaves can be cooked for greens in spring') and Woodland Trust ('can be nibbled raw'). Each preparation method has only one source, so the note just says 'can be eaten'. Nuts: NC State ('edible if cooked properly') and Woodland Trust (roasted, coffee substitute). Dropped from the poisonous field: NC State says raw or unripe beechnuts in large amounts can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach pain and nausea in people and dogs ('low severity'). That is the only source I could open (Woodland Trust's page says nothing on toxicity). It is a reasonable caution, and a second source would let you add it back as a low-risk note. Woodland Trust mentions an old leaf poultice for swellings (one source), so medicinal is left empty. Regex: 'fagus' also matches 'Nothofagus', and 'beech' matches 'Antarctic Beech'. These go to the Southern beech row in the mapping, so make sure that row is matched before this one. Watch for 'hornbeam' too: it doesn't contain 'beech', but the mapping puts Hornbeam on the Pine row, which looks like a bug outside this batch.

name: Oak
edible: Acorns have been eaten after their bitter tannins are removed by soaking or boiling in many changes of water. They can then be ground into flour for bread, or roasted as a coffee substitute. Do not eat raw acorns: they can cause stomach pain and upset.
medicinal: Oak bark is rich in tannins, which tighten skin and gut linings (an astringent effect). It is a recognised traditional European herbal medicine for mild diarrhoea and minor inflammation of the mouth or skin. This rests on long use, not clinical trials. EU regulators advise against it in pregnancy and for under-18s.
poisonous: Acorns, buds and young leaves contain tannins. In people, eating raw acorns can cause stomach pain, constipation and diarrhoea, but serious harm is unlikely. The main risk is to grazing animals: cattle, sheep and horses that eat a lot of oak, often when other food is short, can suffer gut and kidney damage that may kill.
research_notes: Round 2. Edible: leaching supported by PFAF and the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center (University of Texas) 'Ask Mr Smarty Plants' page, which quotes published foraging guides; flour by PFAF and Woodland Trust; coffee substitute by PFAF and NC State; raw-acorn stomach upset by NC State and PFAF hazards. Sources are general to oaks or to Q. robur; red-oak-group acorns (rubra, palustris, coccinea, phellos) are said to be more bitter but I found no two sources, so not stated. Medicinal: the EMA monograph covers Q. robur, Q. petraea and Q. pubescens bark only; it also says not for under-18s or in pregnancy/breastfeeding, but that is a single source (EMA) so it is left out of the note - consider adding as an EMA-only caution. Wild Food UK oak page was blocked. Poisonous: animal toxicity from MSD Veterinary Manual and USDA ARS; horses also named by NC State. REGEX PROBLEM still stands: Evergreen (holm) oak, Quercus ilex (356 trees) falls under Holly because 'ilex' matches; suggest Holly regex 'ilex aquifolium|\bholly\b' (or a negative lookbehind for 'quercus '). | FACT-CHECK: pregnancy/under-18 caution comes from the EMA monograph only; kept because it errs towards safety.

name: Lime (linden)
medicinal: Dried flowers of common, small-leaved and large-leaved lime make lime-flower tea (tilleul). It is a traditional remedy for cold symptoms, mild stress and poor sleep. EU regulators accept these uses on long traditional use only, not on trial evidence.
research_notes: Edible field emptied: young leaves as salad are in PFAF only (Woodland Trust lime pages do not mention eating leaves). The EMA monograph covers only T. cordata, T. platyphyllos and T. x vulgaris (= T. europaea, common lime), so the note names those; it does not apply to silver, Caucasian or American lime, which are also on this row. 'Traditional use only' is from the EMA monograph alone (both EMA URLs are the same agency); the EMA monograph also says use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not recommended and not under age 4 (single agency source, so not included - owner may wish to add). PFAF warns that tea from old flowers may cause 'narcotic' effects (single source, dropped). Regex 'lime' is unanchored and would match any name containing 'lime'.

name: Birch
edible: In early spring, before the leaves open, birch trunks can be tapped for sap. The sap is drunk fresh or boiled down into syrup, which takes a very large amount of sap because it is only slightly sweet.
medicinal: Silver and downy birch leaf is a traditional herbal medicine used to increase urine flow and flush the urinary tract in minor urinary problems. Its use rests on long tradition, not clinical trials. It is not suitable for people with serious heart or kidney disease.
research_notes: Round 2. Edible now sourced: PFAF, University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension, and Cornell Maple Program (which says any birch species can be tapped, so it fits the row). Sources disagree on tree care: PFAF says fill the tap hole and that heavy tapping kills the tree; UAF currently recommends leaving the hole unplugged and only one tap per tree per year. So tree-care advice was left out. Consider adding a site-wide line that street and park trees must not be tapped. Medicinal kept from round 1 (EMA Betulae folium + PFAF), reworded to 'silver and downy birch leaf' because EMA covers only B. pendula and B. pubescens. Still dropped: betulin/salicylates in bark and chaga fungus (no sources).

name: Chitalpa
research_notes: No edible, medicinal or toxic content found; I could not open a reputable page (NC State URL failed). Suggest latin 'x Chitalpa tashkentensis' (mapping spells it 'taschkentensis'). Regex 'desert willow' is loose: true desert willow is Chilopsis linearis, one parent of Chitalpa. Consider removing this row from the map layers since all fields are empty.

name: Willow
medicinal: Willow bark contains salicin, a chemical similar to aspirin. It is a recognised herbal medicine for short-term lower back pain, with moderate evidence from trials; evidence for arthritis is mixed. It is not for children. Avoid it if you are sensitive to aspirin, pregnant, or have a bleeding disorder.
research_notes: Round 2. Medicinal sourced from EMA Salicis cortex summary (well-established use for short-term lower back pain; not for children, aspirin/NSAID allergy, clotting disorders, third trimester), MedlinePlus willow bark (salicin similar to aspirin; possibly effective for back pain; avoid in aspirin sensitivity, pregnancy, children, bleeding disorders) and a PubMed systematic review (moderate evidence for back pain, conflicting for osteoarthritis). MedlinePlus covers several willow species (white, crack, purple, black), so the note fits the row. The aspirin-history / 1763 Royal Society claim was dropped (no two sources opened). No edible or poisonous content found. Regex note from round 1 still applies: 'willow' also matches Willow Oak (Quercus phellos), Desert Willow (Chitalpa) and willow-leaved pear and cotoneaster; make sure those rows are matched before Willow.

name: Poplar
research_notes: Round 2: still all empty. No EMA monograph exists for poplar bud (Populi gemma) - a search found only non-reputable sites. Round 1 findings stand: only PFAF supports the balm-of-Gilead bud uses and salicin, and these are specific to balsam poplar (P. balsamifera, P. x jackii), which is 25 of about 2,100 poplars on the map. the Woodland Trust and NC State pages checked in round 1 give no food or medicinal use. Suggest leaving Poplar off all layers.

name: Zelkova
research_notes: Not researched: my web-search allowance ran out first. To my knowledge Zelkova serrata and Z. carpinifolia have no meaningful edible, medicinal or poisonous use. That is unverified, so all fields stay empty. Suggested latin: 'Zelkova spp.' (Japanese Elm Z. serrata 9 trees, Caucasian Elm Z. carpinifolia 5). Consider dropping this row from the layers if it stays empty.

name: Elm
research_notes: All three fields are empty. Edible: I found no reputable source saying people eat the seeds of English, wych, small-leaved or Dutch elm. Woodland Trust (English and wych elm) and NC State (U. glabra) mention seeds only as wildlife food. Medicinal: the old slippery elm note is about Ulmus rubra, a North American species that is NOT in the map, so it does not apply to this row. NC State's U. rubra page confirms the inner bark is used in throat lozenges, if you ever add that species. Recommend dropping Elm from the edible and medicinal layers. Regex: '\belm\b' also matches 'Japanese Elm' and 'Caucasian Elm' (both Zelkova). The mapping sends them to the Zelkova row, so keep that row ahead of this one.

name: Alder
research_notes: Round 2: all fields left empty. PFAF (Alnus glutinosa) lists the bark as astringent and says fresh bark causes vomiting, but gives no second source; the Woodland Trust alder page mentions only the folk belief that leaves in shoes cool tired feet, and no food, medicinal or toxic use. I could not find a second reputable source for the old 'astringent gargle' note, so it is dropped. Suggest leaving Alder off all layers.
